# Sketching a Carpentry Profile

A sketch is a 2D profile plus the rules that hold it together. The goal is not
to draw a pretty shape; it is to draw a shape that rebuilds correctly when a
dimension changes.

## What you will learn

- How sketch planes map to plan and elevation.
- The geometry tools used for most carpentry parts.
- How constraints and dimensions control a profile.
- How to tell when a sketch is ready to extrude.

## The sketch is a profile

Most carpentry solids start as one closed loop:

- a post cross-section (square or rectangular);
- a rail or joist section (rectangle);
- a picket (rectangle, optionally with a shaped top);
- a notch or cut-out (a closed profile that removes material);
- a roof profile (a triangle or a pair of sloped lines).

Open profiles can be useful for reference geometry, but they cannot become a
solid until they enclose an area.

## Planes in a Z-up world

SolidCraft uses Z as up. The three standard sketch planes are:

| Plane | What it shows | Typical carpentry use |
|-------|---------------|-----------------------|
| XY | Plan view | post layout, deck framing, fence run |
| XZ | Front elevation | wall outline, gate frame, roof profile |
| YZ | Side elevation | shed end wall, stair stringer |

You can also sketch on a face of an existing body. That is how you add a notch
to a post or a bolt hole to a rail: attach the new sketch to the face where the
feature belongs.

## Geometry you will actually use

- **Line** for open outlines, diagonals, and custom profiles.
- **Rectangle** for posts, rails, joists, and pickets.
- **Circle** for bolts, washers, and round posts.
- **Arc** for arched openings and decorative picket tops.
- **Construction geometry** for centrelines and reference distances that
  should not become part of the profile.

Resist the urge to model every chamfer, roundover, and decorative curve. Model
the features that affect fit, assembly, or the cut list. A little cosmetic
detail is useful for communication; a fully sculpted board is usually wasted
effort.

## Constraints are the rules

Constraints tell the solver what must remain true:

- horizontal or vertical;
- coincident (two points together);
- parallel or perpendicular;
- equal length or radius;
- tangent;
- midpoint;
- symmetry;
- fixed.

A sketch with no constraints can still look right and behave badly: drag one
line and the shape collapses. Constraints are what make the profile survive an
edit.

## Dimensions drive the sketch

A dimension is a number with a name and a value. Driving dimensions control the
geometry; driven (reference) dimensions report it.

Dimension the things that matter:

- overall width and height;
- the size of a notch or mortise;
- the spacing between repeated features;
- the thickness of a rail or picket.

Do not dimension the same distance twice. That is the usual cause of an
over-constrained sketch: two dimensions and a constraint all try to control the
same degree of freedom. If the solver refuses a dimension, remove a redundant
one or convert it to a driven dimension.

## Fully constrained is a checkpoint, not a goal

A fully constrained sketch has zero degrees of freedom. That is a good
checkpoint before extruding, but it is not a moral requirement. A sketch can be
under-constrained and still produce the right part if the missing freedom does
not matter. What matters is that the dimensions you care about cannot drift.

## Build along: a post section

1. Create a sketch on XY.
2. Draw a rectangle from `(0, 0)` to `(90, 90)`.
3. Constrain the bottom edge horizontal and the left edge vertical.
4. Dimension the width and height to 90 mm.
5. Confirm the solver reports zero degrees of freedom and one closed profile.
6. Finish the sketch.

## Checks

- One closed profile.
- No loose line ends.
- Width and height both driven by dimensions, not by accidental snapping.
- The origin is at the corner you intend to use as the datum.

## Exercises

1. Draw a 45 × 140 mm rail section with the long side vertical.
2. Draw a 19 × 140 mm picket with a 45° chamfer on the top two corners.
3. Draw a 90 × 90 mm post with a 45 × 45 mm notch in one corner. Keep the
   notch dimensions parametric.
4. Deliberately over-constrain a rectangle, then repair it without redrawing.

## Next

A closed sketch is only a profile. The next chapter turns profiles into boards,
cuts, and holes.
